content.tldr: RSA is a versatile public-key algorithm supporting encryption, key transport, and digital signatures, whereas Diffie-Hellman is a dedicated key-agreement protocol allowing parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel.
content.simple_explanation: RSA relies on the computational difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. In RSA key exchange, one party generates a symmetric key, encrypts it with the other party's public key, and sends it. Diffie-Hellman (DH) relies on the discrete logarithm problem (or elliptic curve discrete log). Neither party transmits the secret; instead, both exchange mathematical public values and combine them with their private values to independently compute the exact same shared secret key.
content.real_world_example: Color mixing: Alice and Bob agree on a common yellow paint; each adds their private color (blue or red) and swaps the mixed paints publicly; each then adds their own private color to the partner's mix, arriving at identical brown paint without an eavesdropper being able to separate the pigments.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: RSA key transport cannot provide Perfect Forward Secrecy because the long-term private key can decrypt historical recordings. Modern security protocols use Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for ephemeral key agreement and restrict RSA (or ECDSA/Ed25519) to identity signatures.
